analysis.one_liner: Charges large data centers and cryptomining operations fees for fossil-fueled electricity and spends the money on clean power and consumer rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced November 20, 2025 with 9 Democratic cosponsors, has been referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and has seen no further action; no Republican has signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clean Cloud Act would put a price on the pollution behind the electricity used by big data centers and cryptomining operations — facilities above 100 kilowatts of computing power. Utilities and facility owners would pay a fee, starting at $20 per ton of greenhouse gas emissions above a regional baseline, rising by $10 plus inflation each year, with the baseline dropping to zero by 2035. The bill bars utilities from recovering the fee by raising rates on ordinary households, and it sends 70% of the money to zero-carbon power and long-duration storage projects, 25% to grants that lower residential electric bills, and 3% to run the program. It would also publish annual data on how much power each major facility uses and from what sources.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential electricity customers, who have been absorbing rate increases as data centers and cryptomining facilities drive up demand — the bill directs a quarter of collected fees into grants that lower household energy costs and bars utilities from shifting the new fees onto non-data-center customers. Communities near revived fossil plants and the broader public gain from reduced emissions, and the zero-carbon power and long-duration storage industries gain a dedicated funding stream.

how_it_helps.text: Sends 25% of collected fees to grants for states, tribes, municipalities, and utilities that lower residential electricity costs, such as through energy savings or direct rebates, explicitly to offset cost increases from data center power use.

Prohibits electric utilities from recouping the fee by raising rates or adding fees on any customer that is not a covered facility, with a penalty of twice the amount recouped if they try — shielding ordinary households from the cost.
Devotes 70% of collected fees to grants, rebates, and low-interest loans for zero-carbon power plants that run year-round and long-duration storage that can discharge for at least 10 hours.

Requires public annual reporting of each covered facility's location, owner, electricity use, power sources, and emissions intensity, closing what the bill's findings call a lack of transparency about the energy behind cryptomining and data centers.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of large data centers and cryptomining facilities, and the utilities that sell them fossil-fueled power. A facility's fee equals its kilowatt-hours above the emissions baseline, times $20 per ton rising by $10 plus inflation each year until 2035, when the baseline reaches zero and any grid emissions are charged. Facilities powered entirely by zero-carbon electricity around the clock are exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large data centers and cryptomining firms

drawbacks.text: The fees could raise the cost of AI and cloud infrastructure in the United States, and the industry argues such costs may push data center investment to countries with looser rules rather than cleaning up the grid.

The bill counts electricity as zero-carbon only under strict conditions — power purchase agreements generally must involve new or saved generation matched hour-by-hour after 2027 — so facilities will face significant compliance and accounting costs even if they buy renewable power today.

The baseline reaches zero in 2035 for every region, meaning a covered facility pays on any grid emissions at all, even in regions that have cleaned up substantially — an absolute standard rather than a relative one.

Utilities that serve covered facilities absorb the fee on their emissions and can only pass it to the data centers themselves, which utilities and some ratepayer advocates may argue distorts rate design or invites disputes over cost allocation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core bargain is to make the industries driving up electricity demand pay the pollution cost of their power and use the money to hold households harmless. The design is unusually protective of ratepayers for an emissions fee: the pass-through ban with a doubled penalty and the 25% consumer rebate carve-out directly target the cost-shift problem. The main real costs are compliance complexity and the risk of discouraging investment; whether those outweigh the household savings depends on how fast data center demand grows, which the bill's own findings put at up to 12% of US electricity use by 2028.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on November 20, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Nine Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors appear on the record.
The committee has scheduled no markup and the full House has taken no vote; the bill sits at the first procedural step.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost on the merits: the bill has not moved, which leaves the status quo in place — large data centers and cryptomining operators continue to draw fossil-heavy power without a fee, and households continue to absorb the resulting rate pressure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, large data center and crypto operators

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Cloud Act of 2025 on November 20, 2025.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on November 20, 2025 — no markup, no hearing, no vote recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All ten initial supporters, including the sponsor and nine cosponsors, are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by the majority party.

industries.industry: Data centers, including AI and cloud computing operators
industries.note: They would face annual fees on every ton of grid or behind-the-meter emissions above a declining regional baseline, reaching zero tolerance by 2035, plus public disclosure of their power sources. Their interest in cheap fossil power runs against ratepayers, who the bill's findings say face rising costs as data centers push demand toward 12% of US electricity by 2028.

The bill's findings fault proof-of-work mining as deliberately energy-intensive and note that retired fossil plants are being brought back online to power it; miners would pay the same per-ton fees. Their low-cost energy strategy is precisely what the bill prices.

Utilities pay the fee on fossil electricity delivered to covered facilities but are barred from recovering it through rates on other customers, on penalty of a doubled fine; they also become eligible for the 25% consumer-cost grants. Their incentive to spread the fee across all ratepayers runs against households, which is why the bill bans it.

industries.industry: Zero-carbon power and long-duration storage developers
industries.note: Seventy percent of collected fees fund research, demonstration, and deployment of firm zero-carbon generation and 10-hour-plus storage through grants, rebates, and loans. Growing this capacity is what allows data centers to expand without raising household emissions or rates.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support, a referral to a committee chaired by the majority party, and no scheduled markup, the bill's realistic path is to die quietly in committee at the end of the 119th Congress, as most single-sponsor energy bills do. A Democratic majority after the 2026 midterms would be needed for it to advance.
